titre: Tan, Broca's Patient, Who Understood Everything
accroche: Louis Leborgne said only “tan,” but he understood what was said to him. His brain, re-examined in 2007, extends beyond the area that Broca gave his name to.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 11, 1861, a 51-year-old man named Leborgne is brought to the infirmary of the Bicêtre hospice in Paris with a gangrenous phlegmon of the entire right lower limb. The surgeon Paul Broca questions him the next day about the origin of his illness. He answers with only one syllable, “tan,” repeated twice, accompanied by a gesture of the left hand.

## A Man Who Understands

Broca learns that this patient lost speech twenty-one years earlier. At the hospice, everyone knows him as Tan. He understands everything said to him, he hears very well, and he always answers “tan, tan,” with varied gestures that let him express most of his ideas. When his mimicry is not understood, he flies into a temper and adds a single strong oath to his vocabulary. His illness had at first taken away speech and nothing else: paralysis of the right arm, then of the leg, came only about ten years later.

This detail is what matters to Broca. To lose articulate language is not to lose intelligence, nor comprehension, nor the movement of the organs of the voice. It is to lose one particular faculty.

## The Autopsy

Leborgne dies on April 17, at eleven in the morning. The autopsy takes place twenty-four hours later. The brain is shown to the Society of Anthropology, then immersed in alcohol. Broca describes a chronic and progressive softening of the left frontal lobe, spreading step by step, and deduces that the starting focus lay in the region of the third frontal convolution. He writes it up in an 1861 article in the *Bulletin de la Société anatomique* (Bulletin of the Anatomical Society).

## What 2007 Changed

Leborgne's brain is preserved. In 2007, Nina Dronkers and her colleagues publish a high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging scan of it, along with that of a second Broca patient. The authors find that the lesions extend markedly toward the internal regions of the brain, beyond the surface lesions Broca described, and that the zone Broca singled out does not correspond exactly to what is now called “Broca's area.”

## What This Shifts

Broca's area is often presented as the center of speech. The founding patient says something else: his lesion was more extensive than the area that bears his name, and the region won its status from a small number of damaged brains, his own first. A map of the brain is thus drawn from accidents, which does not make it an exact map.

repere.texte: Leborgne had lost speech twenty-one years before Broca examined him: he understood everything said to him, but always answered “tan, tan,” with gestures to express his ideas.
repere.source: Broca, Bulletin de la Société anatomique, 36, 1861, pp. 330-357

carte.punch: He said only “tan,” but understood everything. His brain founded Broca's area.
carte.idee: Louis Leborgne dies on April 17, 1861, at Bicêtre. Broca locates his lesion in the left frontal lobe. In 2007, an MRI of his brain shows damage more extensive than the area that now bears Broca's name.

quiz.question: What does the MRI of Leborgne's brain published in 2007 show?
choix: That the lesion was strictly confined to the area now called Broca's area
That Leborgne in fact had no brain lesion visible on modern imaging
That the lesion extended in depth, beyond the surface described by Broca
That his lesion was in the right frontal lobe, not the left
quiz.explication: The authors find damage markedly more extensive than the surface lesions Broca saw, and a mismatch between the zone he singled out and the so-called Broca's area. Nothing points to an absence of lesion, and the lesion Broca described is in the left hemisphere.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What brings Leborgne to the infirmary of the Bicêtre hospice in April 1861?
choix: A gangrenous phlegmon of the right lower limb
An epileptic seizure that struck in the middle of the street
A fall that caused a fractured skull
A typhoid fever diagnosed by Broca himself
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text places Leborgne's arrival at Bicêtre on account of this gangrenous phlegmon of the right lower limb, not a seizure, a fall, or a fever, none of which is mentioned in Broca's account.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long after the loss of speech did Leborgne's right arm paralysis appear?
choix: Immediately, the very day speech was lost
It never appeared, only the leg was affected
A few weeks later, before arriving at Bicêtre
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that paralysis of the right arm, then of the leg, came only about ten years after the initial loss of speech, and not immediately or a few weeks before Bicêtre.
